title: Report on Studying at Tulane and Vienna
paragraphs: Even a few days after returning to Japan, I feel as if I have not yet come down from the excited state I kept feeling for three months in a foreign land. I had the opportunity to study abroad for two months, in April and May, at Tulane University in the US, and for one month, in June, at the Medical University of Vienna in Austria. I aspired to this study abroad because of a vague wish to see high-quality American medicine and an interest in European general practice.

In my first month at Tulane University, I was in endocrinology. Specifically, I observed the fellows' outpatient clinics and followed up the inpatients I was in charge of. I also went to the clinic twice a week, where I took the history and did the physical examination of outpatients and gave a presentation to the attending that included the differential diagnosis. Also, when I went to a patient's room, there were often doctors from other departments there, and I was surprised that a single patient was being followed by so many specialists.

In the second month I rotated through neurology. Here I was assigned to the stroke team and followed up several post-stroke patients every day. General management was required here, so besides the neurological examination I had to understand vital signs and lab data, the whole-body physical examination and, in some cases, even drug blood concentrations, and I was desperate to get used to it. Also, I had to pick up information from paper charts that were written in cursive and hard to read, which took time, so I went to the ward at 5 a.m. and prepared my presentation before the pre-round with the resident. After that we did rounds with the attending, and if there was a new patient we went to the ER on the spot, so it was a clerkship in which I was pressed for time. However, joining the team as a medical student and receiving all sorts of teaching about cases from the residents when they had time gave me a great sense of fulfilment.

By taking part in these two months of clerkships as a medical student, I learned two things. The first is about American medicine. Medicine in which many differentiated specialists simultaneously follow their own specialty areas for a single patient may indeed provide high-quality care when viewed from that point alone. However, in the present situation, increasing differentiation raises doctors' labour costs and testing costs and leads to higher medical expenses, and access to care for the uninsured is becoming ever more distant. I was surprised at the situation in America, which provides advanced and expensive care to a relatively wealthy group while being unable to provide adequate care to the poor group who cannot obtain insurance. The second is about American medical education. I think it is worth respecting that a thorough educational system has been established in which residents teach medical students and attendings teach residents. What also impressed me was that, within the education, when the attending gave feedback on a case presented by a medical student or resident, he referred to papers and persuaded those around him while valuing EBM.

In the third month, I was in general practice at the Medical University of Vienna. Here, instead of a ward, I stayed as a homestay guest with general practitioners in the Austrian countryside and immersed myself in the life of a practitioner around the clock. The doctor saw about 50 to 80 patients a day and, for patients who found it difficult to come to the clinic because of physical problems, made house calls promptly. Surprisingly, the doctor knew the past history and family background of every person in the village, and to be honest I was overwhelmed by the way he came to feel a strong sense of responsibility for the health of the residents. From this experience, I even came to think that the ability to respond quickly to the various complaints and problems of various patients may come from a sense of responsibility.

What was the most meaningful thing to learn through these three months is that, although healthcare systems differ from country to country, there is a separate yardstick for measuring a good doctor. On this study abroad I was able to meet really many doctors. They included not only the professors of Tulane University and the Austrian general practitioners, but also Japanese doctors working as clinicians overseas, and doctors who contribute to medicine through the United Nations and through research. Through meeting such people, I came to the idea that a good doctor is one who has a strong sense of responsibility for people's health. I think it was a truly valuable experience to be able to reach this conclusion by meeting doctors working overseas.

Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt gratitude to everyone who supported me through this exchange program, especially Dr. 粕谷 and 山崎さん, who advised me many times despite being busy, everyone in the International Exchange Office, the professors who gave lectures, and my friends who encouraged one another during the study abroad. Thank you.
